injected_errors.original_span: No. The significance level alpha is the predefined decision threshold. The p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining the observed test statistic or something more extreme.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. The p-value is the predefined decision threshold. Alpha is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining the observed test statistic or something more extreme.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted text reverses the roles of alpha and the p-value.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Alpha is the predefined significance threshold, whereas the p-value is computed from the null distribution for the observed result or something more extreme.
injected_errors.definition_support: The p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining the observed test statistic or something more extreme. The significance level, α, is a predefined threshold used to decide whether a p-value is statistically significant.

injected_errors.original_span: For a one-sided test at alpha=0.05, the full critical probability 0.05 is placed in one tail. In a symmetric two-sided test at the same alpha, it is split into 0.025 in each tail.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: For a one-sided test at alpha=0.05, the critical probability is split into 0.025 in each tail. In a symmetric two-sided test at the same alpha, the full 0.05 is placed in one tail.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corruption swaps how alpha is allocated between one-sided and two-sided tests.
injected_errors.correct_concept: A one-sided test places all alpha in one tail, while a symmetric two-sided test divides alpha between two tails.
injected_errors.definition_support: For a significance level α, a one-sided test places the critical probability α in one tail, whereas a two-sided test divides the critical probability between the two tails.

injected_errors.original_span: A perfect classifier has AUC 1, while random guessing has AUC 0.5.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: A perfect classifier has AUC 0.9, while random guessing has AUC 0.4.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted text gives incorrect benchmark AUC constants.
injected_errors.correct_concept: A perfect classifier has AUC 1 and random guessing has AUC 0.5.
injected_errors.definition_support: A perfect classifier achieves an AUC of 1, while an algorithm performing random guessing results in an AUC of 0.5.

injected_errors.original_span: First randomly divide the labeled data into disjoint training and test sets. Next induce the classifier from the training set. Finally evaluate its error on the test set as an estimate of generalization error.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: First randomly divide the labeled data into disjoint training and test sets. Next evaluate test-set error with the untrained model. Finally induce the classifier from the training set using that test result.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted procedure evaluates the test set before inducing the model from training data.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Holdout first splits the data, then induces the model from training data, then evaluates it on test data.
injected_errors.definition_support: In this procedure, a labeled set is randomly divided into two disjoint sets: a training set and a test set. A classification model is induced from the training set, and the resulting error rate on the test set is then used as an estimate of the generalization error rate.

injected_errors.original_span: No. A larger AUC summarizes better aggregate behavior, but it does not imply superiority at every operating point when ROC curves intersect. Pointwise dominance is a stronger condition than having a larger area.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. A larger AUC guarantees superiority at every operating point, including cases where the two ROC curves intersect. The area ranking therefore settles every threshold-specific comparison.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted statement extends an aggregate AUC comparison to every operating point even when ROC curves intersect.
injected_errors.correct_concept: A higher AUC does not guarantee pointwise superiority unless one ROC curve strictly dominates the other.
injected_errors.definition_support: A higher AUC for one algorithm does not necessarily mean it is always better than another unless its ROC curve strictly dominates the other across all operating points.

injected_errors.original_span: No. Bootstrap forms training samples by drawing instances with replacement, whereas random subsampling repeats the holdout procedure with random train-test partitions.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: No. Random subsampling forms training samples by drawing instances with replacement, whereas bootstrap repeats the holdout procedure with random train-test partitions.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted text attributes bootstrap's with-replacement sampling mechanism to random subsampling and gives bootstrap the repeated-holdout role.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Bootstrap samples with replacement; random subsampling is repeated holdout.
injected_errors.definition_support: Bootstrap sampling is a technique where training sets are formed by sampling instances with replacement from the original training data.

injected_errors.original_span: No. Random subsampling is the repeated holdout method, so the holdout procedure is performed several times rather than only once.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. Random subsampling is simply one random holdout split, so the holdout procedure is performed once and the resulting test error is the final estimate.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The tutor falsely agrees that random subsampling consists of only one holdout split.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Random subsampling repeats the holdout method several times.
injected_errors.definition_support: Random subsampling, also referred to as the repeated holdout method, is an approach where the holdout method is performed several times.

injected_errors.original_span: No. Increasing the threshold reduces the number of instances predicted positive and causes recall to decrease. Lowering the threshold usually increases recall because more actual positives can be included among the predicted positives.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. Increasing the threshold reduces the number of instances predicted positive and causes recall to increase. Lowering the threshold usually decreases recall because more actual positives are excluded from the predicted positives.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corruption reverses the direction of the threshold-recall relationship.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Raising the threshold causes recall to decrease; lowering it usually increases recall.
injected_errors.definition_support: Increasing the threshold reduces the number of predicted positives and causes recall to decrease.

injected_errors.original_span: No. Internal indices rely only on information in the dataset itself and do not require external class labels.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. Internal indices require external class labels rather than relying only on information in the dataset itself.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted statement reverses the defining information source of internal cluster-validity indices.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Internal indices use only information contained in the dataset and require no external class labels.
injected_errors.definition_support: These indices are characterized by the fact that they rely exclusively on information present within the data set itself, without requiring external information.

injected_errors.original_span: Take every cross-cluster pair with one point in Ci and one in Cj, sum their proximities, and divide by |Ci|*|Cj|.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Take every cross-cluster pair with one point in Ci and one in Cj, sum their proximities, and divide by |Ci|+|Cj|.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted formula uses the sum of cluster sizes instead of the number of cross-cluster pairs.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Group-average linkage divides the sum of all cross-cluster proximities by |Ci||Cj|.
injected_errors.definition_support: proximity(Ci, Cj) = [sum over x in Ci and y in Cj of proximity(x,y)] / (|Ci||Cj|).

injected_errors.original_span: The silhouette coefficient ranges from -1 to 1.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: The silhouette coefficient ranges from -0.5 to 0.5.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted text gives the wrong endpoints for the silhouette coefficient's range.
injected_errors.correct_concept: The silhouette coefficient ranges from -1 to 1.
injected_errors.definition_support: The resulting value of the silhouette coefficient varies between -1 and 1.

injected_errors.original_span: Sequential Forward Generation starts with an empty selected set. At each step it chooses the next best feature, adds it to the selected set S, and removes it from the remaining feature set F.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Sequential Forward Generation starts with an empty selected set. At each step it removes the next best feature from the remaining set F, evaluates the reduced set, and only afterward adds that feature to S.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted version changes the stated order of the SFG update by removing and evaluating before adding the chosen feature to S.
injected_errors.correct_concept: SFG chooses the next best feature, adds it to S, and removes it from F.
injected_errors.definition_support: At each step, it chooses the next best feature according to a specified criterion, adds that feature to the selected set S, and removes it from the remaining feature set F.

injected_errors.original_span: No. Exhaustive search guarantees optimality by visiting all possible states. That guarantee does not extend to heuristic search, which deliberately avoids brute-force enumeration.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. Exhaustive search guarantees optimality, and that guarantee also extends to heuristic search because the heuristic simply reaches the same optimum with fewer visited states.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corruption extends exhaustive search's optimality guarantee to heuristic search.
injected_errors.correct_concept: The stated optimality guarantee belongs to exhaustive search, not heuristic search generally.
injected_errors.definition_support: Exhaustive search is a method used to guarantee optimality by visiting all possible states. While it is the only approach that provides such a guarantee, it is possible to find an optimal subset without visiting every state by employing exact algorithms, such as branch and bound or backtracking.

injected_errors.original_span: A redundant feature overlaps substantially with information already carried by other features. An irrelevant feature provides almost no useful information for the particular data-mining task.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: A redundant feature provides almost no useful information for the task. An irrelevant feature mainly duplicates information already carried by other features.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corruption assigns the defining property of irrelevant features to redundant features and vice versa.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Redundant features provide overlapping information; irrelevance concerns lack of useful task information.
injected_errors.definition_support: Redundant features are those that provide overlapping information.

injected_errors.original_span: No. Redundancy means overlapping information, often because features are strongly correlated. Irrelevance means the feature provides almost no useful information for the task.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. Redundancy means the feature provides almost no useful information for the task, so a redundant feature and an irrelevant feature are effectively the same concept.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The tutor falsely endorses the student's claim that redundancy means lack of useful information.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Redundancy means overlapping information rather than simple irrelevance.
injected_errors.definition_support: Redundant features are those that provide overlapping information.

injected_errors.original_span: No. A larger chi-squared value indicates a greater departure from independence because the observed counts differ more strongly from the counts expected under independence.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. A larger chi-squared value indicates a closer fit to independence because the observed counts are aligning more strongly with the counts expected under independence.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corruption reverses how the chi-squared statistic relates to departure from independence.
injected_errors.correct_concept: A larger chi-squared statistic indicates a greater departure from independence.
injected_errors.definition_support: A larger χ² value indicates a greater departure from independence.

injected_errors.original_span: No. A ranker is a subcategory of filter-based feature selection. It scores individual features using a chosen criterion and orders them by those scores.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. A ranker is a subcategory of wrapper-based feature selection. It scores individual features through the predictive learner and orders them by those model-based scores.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted text places a ranker in the wrapper family instead of the filter family.
injected_errors.correct_concept: A ranker is a filter subcategory that scores and orders individual features.
injected_errors.definition_support: A ranker is a subcategory of filter-based feature selection that evaluates individual features using a chosen criterion, assigns each feature a score, and orders the features according to those scores.

injected_errors.original_span: A filter selects features before the learning algorithm is applied.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: A filter selects features after the learning algorithm is applied.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted definition reverses the timing of filter selection relative to model learning.
injected_errors.correct_concept: A filter performs feature selection before the learning algorithm is applied.
injected_errors.definition_support: The filter approach is a feature selection method that selects features before the learning algorithm is applied.

injected_errors.original_span: F(i,j)=2*precision(i,j)*recall(i,j)/(precision(i,j)+recall(i,j)).
injected_errors.corrupted_span: F(i,j)=2*precision(i,j)*recall(i,j)/(precision(i,j)-recall(i,j)).
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted F-measure formula subtracts recall from precision in the denominator instead of adding them.
injected_errors.correct_concept: F-measure divides twice the precision-recall product by precision plus recall.
injected_errors.definition_support: F(i, j) = 2 × precision(i, j) × recall(i, j) divided by precision(i, j) + recall(i, j).

injected_errors.original_span: A pure cluster has entropy 0.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: A pure cluster has entropy 1.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corruption gives the wrong entropy value for a pure cluster.
injected_errors.correct_concept: A pure cluster has entropy 0.
injected_errors.definition_support: Lower entropy indicates greater class purity, and an entropy of 0 indicates that a cluster contains objects from only one class.

injected_errors.original_span: First partition the labeled data into k folds. Then perform k runs, each time training on k-1 folds and testing on the remaining fold. Finally aggregate the k test performances.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: First aggregate the k test performances into one overall estimate. Then partition the data into k folds and perform the training and testing runs that justify that already-computed aggregate.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corrupted procedure aggregates test performance before the folds and evaluation runs that generate those performances.
injected_errors.correct_concept: k-fold first creates folds, then performs the k train-test runs, then aggregates their performance.
injected_errors.definition_support: k-Fold cross-validation is a method for evaluating model performance that involves segmenting labeled data into k equal-sized partitions, known as folds. The procedure consists of k runs; in each run, one partition is designated as the test set while the remaining partitions serve as the training set. A different model is learned during every run, and the performance of these k models on their respective test folds is aggregated to compute an overall test error rate.

injected_errors.original_span: No. A wrapper's primary goal is predictive performance for a specific, fixed learning algorithm, so the selected subset is learner-specific rather than guaranteed optimal for every other learner.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. Once a wrapper finds the best subset for one fixed learner, that subset can be treated as optimal for every other learning algorithm because wrapper selection is learner-independent.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corruption generalizes a learner-specific wrapper result to all learning algorithms.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Wrapper feature selection is optimized for a specific fixed learner and does not guarantee the same subset is optimal for other learners.
injected_errors.definition_support: Its primary goal is to achieve the highest possible predictive accuracy for a specific, fixed learning algorithm.

injected_errors.original_span: No. A ranker evaluates individual features, assigns each a score, and returns an ordered list. A wrapper evaluates candidate subsets using the predictive performance of a chosen learner.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. A ranker evaluates candidate feature subsets jointly through the predictive performance of the chosen learner, while a wrapper mainly scores individual features and returns an ordered list.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The corruption assigns wrapper-style subset evaluation to the ranker and ranker-style individual scoring to the wrapper.
injected_errors.correct_concept: A ranker scores individual features and orders them; it is not defined as learner-based subset evaluation.
injected_errors.definition_support: A ranker is a subcategory of filter-based feature selection that evaluates individual features using a chosen criterion, assigns each feature a score, and orders the features according to those scores.

injected_errors.original_span: No. Wrappers require greater computational cost because they repeatedly use the target learner to evaluate subsets, and they can be more susceptible to overfitting. Filters are generally faster and cheaper.
injected_errors.corrupted_span: Yes. Wrappers are generally computationally cheaper because they use the target learner directly, and they are less susceptible to overfitting than filters.
injected_errors.what_is_wrong: The tutor falsely endorses the student's claim that wrappers are cheaper and less prone to overfitting.
injected_errors.correct_concept: Wrappers are computationally more expensive and can be more susceptible to overfitting than filters.
injected_errors.definition_support: Wrapper methods use the target learning algorithm itself to evaluate candidate feature subsets. This allows them to exploit the characteristics of a particular learner and potentially obtain better feature subsets for that learner, but they require greater computational cost and can be more susceptible to overfitting.
